idiom_name: function withResource(open, close, body) { try { return body(r) } finally { close(r) } }
implementation_notes: JavaScript passes functions naturally, so the classic structure is written as a helper that opens the resource, calls body(resource) inside a try block and closes it in finally, returning whatever the body returned; an async protocol awaits the body inside the same bracket. What replaces the Smalltalk form is that local idiom rather than a language feature - the language only gained a bracket of its own with the using declaration and Symbol.dispose, which is recent, so most deployed code still writes the helper. Keep the helper when several call sites share a policy or when the protocol is more than disposal (transaction, retry, metrics); inline try/finally when there is a single call site and nothing to share.
pitfalls: finally runs on return and throw but not when the process exits or a promise never settles; an async body must be awaited inside an async wrapper, or the resource is closed while the work is still running.
A teardown that throws inside finally replaces the body's error, so the original failure disappears from the stack.

Capturing the resource in a long-lived closure (an event listener, a timer, a module-level function) defeats the bracket: the handle stays reachable after the call, and disposal either never happens or happens while it is still in use.

variants.name: using / await using with Symbol.dispose and DisposableStack
variants.idiom_name: using resource = disposable; and await using for Symbol.asyncDispose
variants.implementation_notes: The explicit resource management feature binds disposal to the lexical scope: the engine calls [Symbol.dispose]() when the scope exits, multiple using declarations dispose in reverse order, and a failure during both the body and disposal is aggregated into a SuppressedError instead of one error masking the other; await using with Symbol.asyncDispose is the asynchronous form, and DisposableStack/AsyncDisposableStack register arbitrary cleanup through use, adopt and defer when no disposable object exists. That is the language absorbing the pattern for single-resource brackets. Availability is recent (Chromium 134 / V8 13.8) and the symbols may need polyfills, so the callback helper remains the portable default; using is the better choice on a modern runtime where the scope really is the resource's lifetime.
pitfalls: using is only allowed inside a block or function body, not at the top level of a script or module, and the binding must be initialised at its declaration.

A reference copied out of the scope outlives disposal: the object is disposed but still reachable, and using it later fails or silently corrupts state - use DisposableStack when disposal must be managed explicitly.
Older runtimes need polyfills for Symbol.dispose, Symbol.asyncDispose, DisposableStack and SuppressedError, and bundlers must not downlevel the declarations away.
